                                         PUC PROJECT NO. 58481


    RULEMAKING    TO   IMPLEMENT                            §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                              §
    STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                           §                     OF TEXAS



    SATOSHI ENERGY COMMENTS ON STAFF'S SECOND DISCUSSION DRAFT ON
        PROJECT NO. 58481, RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD
             INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561


                                               1. INTRODUCTION


           Satoshi Energy develops colocated renewable energy and data center infrastructure across

ERCOT and other markets. By partnering closely with both generation asset owners and data

center operators, the company provides a comprehensive approach to interconnection planning and

execution of large load projects. Satoshi Energy has energized 476 megawatts (MW) of data center

facilities colocated with existing renewable generation assets in ERCOT, which comprises nearly

10% of all large loads energized in ERCOT as of 2025.1 The company is actively advancing an

additional 5 gigawatts (GW) in its ERCOT pipeline. This scale of experience positions Satoshi

Energy as an industry leader of net metering arrangements at scale, bringing investment,

innovation, and high-quality infrastructure to Texas while supporting ERCOT reliability and

economic growth.


           Satoshi Energy appreciates the Commission’s efforts to implement PURA §37.0561 and

define the Large Load Interconnection Study (LLIS) process to support grid reliability and

ensure that interconnecting loads contribute appropriately to transmission costs. We encourage



1
    ERCOT. (2025). (rep.). Large Load Interconnection Status Update. Retrieved 2025,.
 the Commission to consider different load configurations with widely variable transmission

costs–some, such as colocated loads, leverage existing infrastructure and do not require system

upgrades, thereby posing minimal risk to stranded transmission costs. Applying uniform security

and procedural requirements without accounting for these distinctions does not create the market

based incentive to seek out projects that minimize transmission upgrades while creating new load

customers that contribute to transmission costs and create economic development with limited

standard asset risk. This proposed structure unintentionally imposes disproportionate burdens on

greenfield development by raising unnecessary early-stage capital requirements and thus limiting

the competitiveness of business development in ERCOT.



                       2. COMMENTS ON PROPOSED 16 TAC §25.194


General Comments


       Satoshi Energy supports the Commission’s objective of discouraging speculative load

requests while preserving ERCOT’s competitiveness as a destination for data center and other

large-load investment. Projects that leverage existing infrastructure, particularly net metering

arrangements, very rarely (to date we have 8 projects totaling 1.2 GW with approved load studies

zero have required CIAC or bulk system upgrades) result in Contribution in Aid of Construction

(CIAC) obligations and therefore present minimal stranded-asset risk. While such projects

should remain liable for costs where they exist, they should not be required to post or hold

substantial security where the underlying risk is absent.


       Satoshi Energy intentionally develops projects that take advantage of existing

transmission facilities and pockets of high generation with low incremental upgrade costs. This is
 an efficient and market-aligned approach to load development that benefits ERCOT by reducing

congestion, minimizing new construction, and encouraging load to locate where it can be

supported with minimal system impact. Accordingly, Satoshi Energy urges the Commission to

size deposits commensurate with risk and to require utilities to hold developer capital only for

the minimum duration necessary to secure against actual cost exposure.


Comments on Section (a): Purpose and Scope

       (a) Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric

       utility, a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative, to interconnect a large load

       customer to the ERCOT transmission network. Any projects that have Planning Studies

       Approved, as defined by ERCOT, prior to the effective date of this rule shall be exempt

       from the following standards and criteria for large load interconnection.


       Satoshi Energy strongly supports clarifying applicability and grandfathering provisions in

§25.194(a). The Commission should explicitly limit new fees, deposits, and procedural

requirements to projects that have not yet received ERCOT approval of Planning Studies as of

the date that this rule for large load interconnection comes into effect. Projects that have already

progressed through ERCOT approval of Planning Studies have engaged extensively with

Transmission Service Providers (TSPs) and ERCOT, made capital deployment decisions, and

structured development timelines based on existing processes. Applying new financial

requirements retroactively to these late-stage projects would unfairly disadvantage developers

who acted in good faith and undermine strong and serious projects that would otherwise come to

fruition. A clear cutoff at ERCOT approval of Planning Studies will allow the Commission to

clear the queue prospectively without disrupting viable projects already well underway. Another

goal from the Commission is to ensure the queue is comprised of high likelihood projects.
 ERCOT recently published that an estimated 5 GW of projects will have planning studies

approved in 2026, with the requested capacity projected to rise slightly to 14 GW in 2030.2 To

put this in context, ERCOT anticipates nearly 209 GW of early-stage projects that have not yet

been approved in 2030 alone.3 This highlights that setting the definition at “Planning Studies

Approved” by ERCOT could clean up the queue to only retain a manageable set of load requests

as compared to the 200+ GW of early-stage projects, some of which may be speculative.


Comments on Section (f) - Intermediate Agreement

       (f) Intermediate Agreement. Before a large load interconnection study is begun Within

       30 days of the commencement of the large load interconnection study, the large load

       customer must execute and securitize an intermediate agreement that, at a minimum,

       includes the updated disclosures and phased financial commitments required under this

       subsection. The interconnecting utility must cancel the interconnection request and notify

       ERCOT of the cancellation if the large load customer fails to execute and securitize an

       intermediate agreement within 30 days of the commencement of the large load

       interconnection study.

               (8) Financial security on a dollar per MW basis. A large load customer must

               pay financial security to the interconnecting utility in two stages, as follows: in

               the amount of $100,000 per MW of the contracted peak demand for new

               interconnection requests or of the incremental increase in the peak demand for

               expanded interconnection requests.

November-2025.pdf.

of projects under “No Studies Submitted” and 76,749 MW of projects within “Under ERCOT Review”
categories in 2030.
 (A) First-stage security. To initiate the planning studies by the

interconnecting utility, the large load customer must post financial security

in the amount of $10,000 per MW of the contracted peak demand for new

interconnection requests or of the incremental increase in the peak

demand. The interconnection utility must complete the studies within 6

months of executing the Intermediate Agreement.

(B) Second-stage security. Within 30 days after receipt of planning study

results, the load customer must post an additional $10,000 per MW to

proceed with ERCOT review of the planning studies.

(C) (A) Beginning in 2027, the commission will adjust the $10,000 per

MW in Stage I and $10,000 per MW in Stage II $100,000 value on

January 1 of each calendar year.

       (i) The annual adjustment will be proportional to the third quarter

       percentage change in the national Consumer Price Index (CPI)

       published by the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of

       Labor Statistics.

       (ii) The executive director must designate a substitute index to be

       used as a reference for adjustments if the CPI becomes

       unavailable.

(D) (B) The balance of any unused study fee that the large load customer

paid to the interconnecting utility under subsection (c) of this section must

be credited towards satisfying the financial security requirements under

this subsection.
                       (E) (C) The interconnecting utility may accept the following forms of

                      payment for the financial security:

                              (i) cash collateral;

                              (ii) corporate or parental guaranty, only if the corporation or parent

                              corporation has a credit rating equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher

                              from Standard & Poor's or Moody's; or

                              (iii) a letter of credit issued by a major U.S. commercial bank, or a

                              U. S. branch office of a major foreign commercial bank, with a

                              credit rating of at least "A-" by Standard & Poor's or "A3" by

                              Moody's Investor Service.

                      (F) (D) If the large load customer provides a corporate or parental

                      guaranty under this subsection, the interconnecting utility may require the

                      submission of financial records or statements to determine the customer's

                      financial stability.


       Satoshi Energy supports the Commission’s intent to require financial commitments at the

Intermediate Agreement stage as a means of ensuring that large load interconnection requests are

supported by serious development intent. A “pay-to-play” framework can be an effective tool to

deter speculative requests and ensure that TSPs and ERCOT are able to deploy resources

efficiently to conduct large load studies. Satoshi Energy proposes sizing the security to $20,000

per MW, a value close to the median of proposals within the December 2025 request for

stakeholder comments and widely requested at the January 9 workshop, in a staged approach.

The first stage requires an initial $10,000/MW deposit to confirm funds prior to planning studies,
 with an additional $10,000/MW required within 30 days of load study completion in order to

move forward with ERCOT review.


       The current draft does not appropriately recognize that development certainty increases

as a project advances through successive interconnection and other milestones. This approach

both incorporates the Commission’s goal of deterring speculative requests while also sizing it

proportionate to project maturity and the actual risks being addressed. Requiring $10,000 per

MW initial security to initiate planning studies appropriately balances the Commission’s interest

in confirming serious requests with the need to preserve access for viable loads. Likewise,

conditioning additional $10,000 security on receipt of load study results ensures that developers

can make informed decisions on system impacts and capacity before committing further capital.

This proposal would still require meaningful capital commitments from serious developers while

preserving competitive market participation to deliver reliable load, economic investment, and

efficient use of the transmission system.


       Satoshi Energy concurs with the statements made by Black Mountain during the January

9 workshop that imposing a $100,000 per MW financial security requirement at the Intermediate

Agreement stage would result in the cancellation of viable projects that would otherwise come to

fruition. This concern is not theoretical. Satoshi Energy currently has multiple gigawatts of

projects in its ERCOT pipeline that would be deferred for several years or abandoned entirely if

such a requirement were adopted. These projects are not speculative; they are carefully sited,

capital-backed developments that rely on existing infrastructure and would proceed under a more

appropriate financial framework.
        Satoshi Energy emphasizes that excessive early-stage financial security does not

distinguish between speculative requests and serious development intent. Rather, speculation is

driven primarily by lack of transparency and uncertainty in the large load interconnection

process. When developers have limited visibility into withdrawal capacity, study timelines, or

whether results will be delivered in weeks or years, rational actors across the market, ranging

from small developers to hyperscalers, are incentivized to submit multiple overlapping requests

to preserve optionality. This dynamic is a direct consequence of a “black box” process, not an

absence of financial commitment. Increasing security levels without addressing underlying

transparency issues risks exacerbating this behavior rather than curbing it.


       We urge Staff to consider that one unintended, but significant consequence of imposing

exorbitant dollar-per-megawatt security requirements is encouraging market consolidation.

Developers with higher costs of capital may be forced to seek acquisition by hyperscale entities

solely to access lower-cost lines of credit, not because of project merit. For many developers,

each additional $10 million in required security (that would be a 500MW project at $20,000 per

MW) translates into approximately $1 million to $1.5 million per year in debt service, materially

altering project economics from meaningful development costs towards paying banks more

money and skewing the market toward entities with the lowest cost of capital rather than the

most efficient or system-aligned projects. A balanced approach to financial security will protect

ratepayers, preserve competition, and ensure that high-quality projects are not lost due to

disproportionate early-stage capital barriers. We strongly advise the PUCT to consider our

proposal to ensure the mandate set forth in PURA §37.0561 to establish a rule that

supports business development in Texas is upheld.
 Section (i) Interconnection agreement.

      (9) Contribution in aid of construction (CIAC). An interconnecting utility must not

      begin construction of facilities to interconnect a large load customer before a large load

      customer pays CIAC in an amount that is equal to the interconnecting utility's estimated

      costs to interconnect the large load customer and that is directly attributable to

      interconnecting the large load customer. The CIAC must be trued up to reflect the

      interconnecting utility' s actual costs once the facilities are completed, and a customer

      may receive a surcharge or refund for the difference in actual costs relative to the

      estimate.

             (A) Costs directly attributable to interconnecting the large load customer include

             all costs associated with transmission facilities built to interconnect the large load

             customer to the existing transmission network, including substation upgrades

             associated with interconnecting the new large load customer.

             (B) The interconnecting utility may accept the following forms of payment for the

             CIAC. CIAC must be paid in the form of a direct cash payment.

                     (i) cash collateral;

                     (ii) corporate or parental guaranty, only if the corporation or parent

                     corporation has a credit rating equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher from

                     Standard & Poor's or Moody's; or

                     (iii) a letter of credit issued by a major U.S. commercial bank, or a U. S.

                     branch office of a major foreign commercial bank, with a credit rating of

                     at least "A-" by Standard & Poor's or "A3" by Moody's Investor Service.
                (B) Costs associated with system upgrades that would not be required but for the

               interconnecting large load customer are costs directly attributable to the

               interconnecting large load customer. Where a system upgrade is necessary to

               serve multiple large load customers, such system upgrade costs must be pro-rated

               among those large load customers based on the contracted peak demand of each

               of those customers.

               (C) For a large load customer that is interconnecting to an existing transmission

               asset, costs directly attributable to interconnecting the large load customer include

               a share of the original CIAC that another large load customer paid under this

               section. The share of original CIAC must be calculated based on remaining net

               book value of the associated costs as a fraction of the original book value of those

               costs, and further pro-rated based on the share of contracted peak demand of the

               new large load customer as a fraction of the aggregate contracted peak demand of

               all large load customers associated with that transmission asset, including the new

               large load customer. CIAC payments under this subsection must be credited to the

               previous large load customers that contributed to the previous CIAC payments, on

               an asset by asset basis, in proportion to those previous payments


       Satoshi Energy agrees with the concerns raised by TSPs and other stakeholders during

the January 9 workshop regarding the complexity introduced by §25.194(i)(9)(B) and (C). While

transmission upgrades may benefit multiple customers, attempting to allocate costs among

projects on a prorated or net book value basis would be extremely difficult to administer and

likely lead to disputes. Satoshi Energy recommends eliminating subsections (i)(9)(B) and (C)

and defaulting to the longstanding ERCOT CIAC framework. The existing approach has enabled
 ERCOT to energize transmission and generation efficiently and has proven far more successful

than allocation regimes in other ISOs. Maintaining the status quo in this case will provide

certainty and avoid unnecessary complexity.


       Satoshi Energy further recommends that the Commission permit large load customers to

satisfy financial obligations under this section through parental guarantees or letters of credit, in

addition to cash payments. Allowing these commonly accepted forms of financial assurance

would provide equivalent protection to interconnecting utilities while avoiding unnecessary

liquidity constraints on developers. Parental guarantees and letters of credit are widely used

across infrastructure and energy markets, provide enforceable credit support backed by

financially capable entities, and allow capital to remain deployed in project development rather

than held idle. Incorporating these alternatives would preserve ratepayer protection, align with

standard commercial practice, and reduce the risk that otherwise viable projects are delayed or

cancelled solely due to rigid cash-only requirements.


Section (l) Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that energizes

       (l) Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that energizes.

       An interconnecting utility must apply the financial security that a large load customer

       paid under this section to any amounts owed for costs incurred by the interconnecting

       utility to fulfill the large load customer's request for interconnection of the contracted

       peak demand. Once the interconnecting utility has completed the facility study that

       determines the CIAC amount, the CIAC obligation supersedes the dollar per MW

       security requirement. Any remaining security balance must be returned to the large load

       customer within 30 days.
                (1) After applying the financial security to any amounts owed, the interconnecting

               utility must refund 20% of the remaining balance when the large load customer

               energizes and ratably as the large load customer meets the milestones identified in

               the customer' s schedule for phased energization of its contracted peak demand.

               (2) The interconnecting utility must refund any remaining balance when the large

               load customer sustains operations for five years at the customer' s contracted peak

               demand.


       Satoshi Energy also emphasizes the importance of clearly integrating dollar-per-

megawatt security with existing cost-recovery mechanisms. Once facility studies are complete

and the Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC) amount is determined, CIAC should

represent the definitive financial obligation associated with transmission upgrades. At that point,

any dollar-based security posted for study purposes and for stranded asset cost no longer serves a

risk-mitigation function and should be returned promptly. Treating CIAC as superseding interim

security avoids duplicative financial requirements and ensures that developer capital is held only

for as long as necessary to address actual stranded-cost exposure. Echoing our past comments

and the points raised by Google, Lancium, and the TSPs at the January 9 workshop, a CIAC

directly addresses risk of stranded asset cost by ensuring transmission upgrades necessary for

interconnection are paid for directly by the customer, thereby not passing it unduly onto

ratepayers. We also highlight Oncor’s comments in the January 9 workshop that the risk of a

customer walking away from approved capacity is extremely low, and TSPs already have a

mechanism to securitize this scenario that has functioned well. We want to highlight the

importance of this to ensure consistency with the mandate set forth in PURA §37.0561 to

establish a rule that supports business development in Texas is upheld. Each additional $10
 million in required security (that would be a 500MW project at $20,000 per MW) translates into

approximately $1 million to $1.5 million per year in debt service, materially altering project

economics from meaningful development costs towards paying banks more money. We strongly

suggest the PUCT to consider our suggestion to ensure capital is efficiently used to promote

business in Texas and protect ratepayers.




                                         3. CONCLUSION


       Satoshi Energy appreciates the Commission’s continued consideration of these important

issues and its engagement with stakeholders throughout this rulemaking. We urge the

Commission to adopt a final rule that calibrates financial and procedural requirements to actual

system impact, preserves access for viable large-load projects, and provides transparency and

predictability in the interconnection process. A balanced, risk-based framework will protect

ratepayers while continuing to support innovation, investment, and reliable load growth in Texas.

LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                    §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                 §                 OF TEXAS


SATOSHI ENERGY COMMENTS ON STAFF'S SECOND DISCUSSION DRAFT ON
    PROJECT NO. 58481, RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD
         INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561

 ● §25.194(a): The Commission should exempt projects that have Planning Studies
   Approved (as historically defined by ERCOT) by the effective date of this rule on Large
   Load Interconnection Standards. Limiting new requirements to projects that have not yet
   secured planning studies approval (an estimated 209 GW in 2030) would focus the LLIS
   framework on early-stage requests and meaningfully reduce speculative queue volume.
 ● §25.194(f): Satoshi Energy supports a “pay-to-play” mechanism at the Intermediate
   Agreement stage through a two-phase financial security structure: an initial $10,000/MW
   deposit to initiate planning studies, followed by an additional $10,000/MW deposit after
   receipt of load study results to proceed with ERCOT review. The combined $20,000/MW
   amount reflects the median stakeholder proposal and appropriately deters speculative
   requests while remaining proportionate to project maturity, system risk, and viable
   economic development.
 ● §25.194(f): The Commission should require that the interconnection utility complete the
   studies within 6 months of executing the Intermediate Agreement.
 ● §25.194(f): Satoshi Energy emphasizes the serious risks of a $100,000 per MW security
   as other stakeholders highlighted at the January 9 workshop: (1) the cancellation or
   deferral of viable projects with serious development intent and (2) driving developers
   toward market consolidation. Excessive dollar per megawatt security requirements
   disproportionately affect developers with higher costs of capital and may force
   acquisition by hyperscale entities solely to access lower-cost financing, skewing the
   market away from efficient, system-aligned projects.
 ● §25.194(i): The Commission should eliminate CIAC allocation provisions in
   §25.194(i)(9)(B) and (C). Pro-rated and net book value allocation of shared system
   upgrades would be difficult to administer and likely lead to disputes. Maintaining the
   longstanding ERCOT CIAC framework provides clarity and administrative efficiency.
 ● §25.194(i): The Commission should allow CIAC and security obligations to be satisfied
   through cash, parental guarantees, or letters of credit.
 ● §25.194(l): The Commission should require a refund of remaining financial security
   within 30 days of CIAC determination. After facility studies establish CIAC, the
   remaining deposit no longer serves a risk-mitigation function as the cost of transmission
   buildout has been securitized. Retaining security beyond this point is duplicative and
  inefficient.
● Overall, Satoshi Energy urges adoption of a risk-based, proportionate LLIS framework. A
  rule that aligns financial and procedural requirements with actual system impact will
  deter speculative requests, protect ratepayers, preserve competitive market participation,
  and support continued business development in Texas as described in PURA §37.0561.

       Satoshi Energy supports the Commission' s intent to require financial commitments at the

Intermediate Agreement stage as a means of ensuring that large load interconnection requests are

supported by serious development intent. A "pay-to-play" framework can be an effective tool to

deter speculative requests and ensure that TSPs and ERCOT are able to deploy resources

efficiently to conduct large load studies. Satoshi Energy proposes sizing the security to $20,000

per MW, a value close to the median of proposals within the December 2025 request for

stakeholder comments and widely requested at the January 9 workshop, in a staged approach.

The first stage requires an initial $10,000/MW deposit to confirm funds prior to planning studies,
 with an additional $10,000/MW required within 30 days of load study completion in order to

move forward with ERCOT review.


       The current draft does not appropriately recognize that development certainty increases

as a project advances through successive interconnection and other milestones. This approach

both incorporates the Commission's goal of deterring speculative requests while also sizing it

proportionate to project maturity and the actual risks being addressed. Requiring $10,000 per

MW initial security to initiate planning studies appropriately balances the Commission' s interest

in confirming serious requests with the need to preserve access for viable loads. Likewise,

conditioning additional $10,000 security on receipt of load study results ensures that developers

can make informed decisions on system impacts and capacity before committing further capital.

This proposal would still require meaningful capital commitments from serious developers while

preserving competitive market participation to deliver reliable load, economic investment, and

efficient use of the transmission system.


       Satoshi Energy concurs with the statements made by Black Mountain during the January

9 workshop that imposing a $100,000 per MW financial security requirement at the Intermediate

Agreement stage would result in the cancellation of viable projects that would otherwise come to

fruition. This concern is not theoretical. Satoshi Energy currently has multiple gigawatts of

proj ects in its ERCOT pipeline that would be deferred for several years or abandoned entirely if

such a requirement were adopted. These proj ects are not speculative; they are carefully sited,

capital-backed developments that rely on existing infrastructure and would proceed under a more

appropriate financial framework.
        Satoshi Energy emphasizes that excessive early-stage financial security does not

distinguish between speculative requests and serious development intent. Rather, speculation is

driven primarily by lack of transparency and uncertainty in the large load interconnection

process. When developers have limited visibility into withdrawal capacity, study timelines, or

whether results will be delivered in weeks or years, rational actors across the market, ranging

from small developers to hyperscalers, are incentivized to submit multiple overlapping requests

to preserve optionality. This dynamic is a direct consequence of a "black box" process, not an

absence of financial commitment. Increasing security levels without addressing underlying

transparency issues risks exacerbating this behavior rather than curbing it.


       We urge Staff to consider that one unintended, but significant consequence of imposing

exorbitant dollar-per-megawatt security requirements is encouraging market consolidation.

Developers with higher costs of capital may be forced to seek acquisition by hyperscale entities

solely to access lower-cost lines of credit, not because of proj ect merit. For many developers,

each additional $10 million in required security (that would be a 500MW project at $20,000 per

MW) translates into approximately $1 million to $1.5 million per year in debt service, materially

altering project economics from meaningful development costs towards paying banks more

money and skewing the market toward entities with the lowest cost of capital rather than the

most efficient or system-aligned proj ects. A balanced approach to financial security will protect

ratepayers, preserve competition, and ensure that high-quality proj ects are not lost due to

disproportionate early-stage capital barriers. We strongly advise the PUCT to consider our

proposal to ensure the mandate set forth in PURA §37.0561 to establish a rule that

supports business development in Texas is upheld.

       Satoshi Energy agrees with the concerns raised by TSPs and other stakeholders during

the January 9 workshop regarding the complexity introduced by §25.194(i)(9)(B) and (C). While

transmission upgrades may benefit multiple customers, attempting to allocate costs among

projects on a prorated or net book value basis would be extremely difficult to administer and

likely lead to disputes. Satoshi Energy recommends eliminating subsections (i)(9)(B) and (C)

and defaulting to the longstanding ERCOT CIAC framework. The existing approach has enabled
 ERCOT to energize transmission and generation efficiently and has proven far more successful

than allocation regimes in other ISOs. Maintaining the status quo in this case will provide

certainty and avoid unnecessary complexity.


       Satoshi Energy further recommends that the Commission permit large load customers to

satisfy financial obligations under this section through parental guarantees or letters of credit, in

addition to cash payments. Allowing these commonly accepted forms of financial assurance

would provide equivalent protection to interconnecting utilities while avoiding unnecessary

liquidity constraints on developers. Parental guarantees and letters of credit are widely used

across infrastructure and energy markets, provide enforceable credit support backed by

financially capable entities, and allow capital to remain deployed in proj ect development rather

than held idle. Incorporating these alternatives would preserve ratepayer protection, align with

standard commercial practice, and reduce the risk that otherwise viable projects are delayed or

cancelled solely due to rigid cash-only requirements.

       Satoshi Energy also emphasizes the importance of clearly integrating dollar-per-

megawatt security with existing cost-recovery mechanisms. Once facility studies are complete

and the Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC) amount is determined, CIAC should

represent the definitive financial obligation associated with transmission upgrades. At that point,

any dollar-based security posted for study purposes and for stranded asset cost no longer serves a

risk-mitigation function and should be returned promptly. Treating CIAC as superseding interim

security avoids duplicative financial requirements and ensures that developer capital is held only

for as long as necessary to address actual stranded-cost exposure. Echoing our past comments

and the points raised by Google, Lancium, and the TSPs at the January 9 workshop, a CIAC

directly addresses risk of stranded asset cost by ensuring transmission upgrades necessary for

interconnection are paid for directly by the customer, thereby not passing it unduly onto

ratepayers. We also highlight Oncor's comments in the January 9 workshop that the risk of a

customer walking away from approved capacity is extremely low, and TSPs already have a

mechanism to securitize this scenario that has functioned well. We want to highlight the

importance of this to ensure consistency with the mandate set forth in PURA §37.0561 to

establish a rule that supports business development in Texas is upheld. Each additional $10
 million in required security (that would be a 500MW project at $20,000 per MW) translates into

approximately $1 million to $1.5 million per year in debt service, materially altering project

economics from meaningful development costs towards paying banks more money. We strongly

suggest the PUCT to consider our suggestion to ensure capital is efficiently used to promote

business in Texas and protect ratepayers.




                                         3. CONCLUSION


       Satoshi Energy appreciates the Commission's continued consideration of these important

issues and its engagement with stakeholders throughout this rulemaking. We urge the

Commission to adopt a final rule that calibrates financial and procedural requirements to actual

system impact, preserves access for viable large-load proj ects, and provides transparency and

predictability in the interconnection process. A balanced, risk-based framework will protect

ratepayers while continuing to support innovation, investment, and reliable load growth in Texas.
